General owner-matching theoremThe argument in bundle member manuscript/owner-matching-proof.tex, Theorem thm:owner-matching, proves the stated inequality for every matching  $R$  in the specified family.Matching size and uncovered verticesEvery odd-order path contributes exactly one uncovered endpoint, including an isolated vertex. Every other owner component is completely covered. Consequently,
$$|W|=2b-o,\qquad |R|=\frac{2b-o}{2}.$$
The parity of the total owner order gives  $o\equiv0\pmod2$ .An independent set  $T\subseteq W$  of  $J_R$  contains at most one endpoint of each  $R$ -edge. Thus one can select an endpoint outside  $T$  from every matching edge and add every uncovered owner. The resulting owner set  $S_C$  satisfies
$$|S_C|
=o+\frac{2b-o}{2}
=\frac{2b+o}{2},
\qquad S_C\cap T=\varnothing.$$
This accounts correctly for the moving uncovered endpoints of odd paths.Owner feasibility, including squaresOn an even-order path, an endpoint-leaving odd-order path, or a non-square even cycle, the complement  $B-R$  is a matching. Since  $S_C$  contains exactly one endpoint of each  $R$ -edge, every edge of  $B[S_C]$  belongs to that complementary matching. Hence  $\Delta(B[S_C])\le1$ .On an owner square,  $R$  consists of its two diagonals. Selecting one endpoint from each diagonal selects exactly two owners; their induced graph has maximum degree at most one. These diagonal pairs are auxiliary pairs between owners of the same physical colour, exactly as required.The endpoint restriction on odd paths is substantive and correctly retained throughout the manuscript and implementation. For example, the maximum matching
$$\{v_0v_1,v_3v_4\}$$
of the path  $v_0v_1v_2v_3v_4$  leaves the interior vertex  $v_2$  uncovered. Its complementary edges  $v_1v_2,v_2v_3$  share a vertex. The specified endpoint-leaving family has the complementary-matching property used in the proof. $K_4$  components and Brooks’s theoremThe simple graph  $J_R$  is a union of three matchings, so  $\Delta(J_R)\le3$ . Repeated  $P/R$  or  $Q/R$  edges contribute one adjacency.A  $K_4$  in  $J_R$  is an entire component. At each of its vertices, three distinct neighbours exhaust the three matching types. Therefore its  $R$ -edges form a perfect matching, and deleting those edges leaves a  $P/Q$  four-cycle.That four-cycle is also an entire component of the original  $P\cup Q$ : every vertex already has its incident  $P$ -edge and  $Q$ -edge inside the four vertices. Restricting to  $W$  therefore creates no additional kind of  $K_4$  obstruction.After removing the  $z$  copies of  $K_4$ , the remaining graph is three-colourable. Brooks applies to connected components of maximum degree three; paths, lower-degree components, and odd cycles admit at most three colours directly. Taking a largest colour class on the remainder and one vertex from each  $K_4$  gives
$$|T|\ge z+\left\lceil\frac{2b-o-4z}{3}\right\rceil.$$
The quantity inside this last ceiling has a nonnegative numerator because the  $K_4$  components are disjoint subsets of  $W$ .Physical compatibility and countingThe selected physical set consists of:all  $b$  helpers;owners indexed by  $S_C$ ;witnesses indexed by  $T$ .Independence in  $P$  gives each helper at most one selected witness. Independence in  $Q$  removes selected witness–witness conflicts. The condition  $S_C\cap T=\varnothing$  removes selected owner–witness conflicts. The remaining selected owner edges lie in  $B[S_C]$ , whose maximum degree is at most one.These three layers are disjoint. Each uncovered owner and each matching edge contributes exactly once. Thus
